A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UTRL research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A.1–A.6 provide readable evidence for a reliable comparison, including material moved or renumbered in v3.

before.justification: v2 reports original UTRL training and evaluation results, comparisons with SFT and CURE, and validity-reward and iterative-training analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds LiveCodeBench evaluation, Llama experiments, reward-weight ablations and additional baseline comparisons.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Equations 1–4 retain the same alternating training procedure, discrimination and validity rewards, validity filtering and code-generator reward. The additional model experiments apply the existing method; best-of-N distillation is a new comparator, not a UTRL component.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on 511 unseen LiveCodeBench-v2 programming tasks beyond v2's 945 TACO evaluation tasks (Section 4.1; Appendix A.2.1; Table 3). This substantially expands independent evaluation coverage within competitive programming. TACO and CodeContests training coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v3 adds Qwen3-32B to Table 1, best-of-N distillation in Table 4, and code-generator controls using ground-truth-code SFT and RL rewards from GPT-4o-generated tests in Figure 7. Its LiveCodeBench comparison also includes untuned Qwen2.5-7B. These broaden the evaluated alternatives beyond the retained SFT, CURE and ground-truth-test comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix A.3 revises the reported Qwen3-4B schedule from 370 to 330 code-generator steps and from 100 to 170 second-iteration tester steps. New protocols include 50-step Llama training, 50-step reward-weight experiments and eight-candidate distillation. These change reported budgets and experimental settings without establishing which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds a discrimination-weight sweep over lambda = 0, 0.85 and 1, measuring downstream code selection and test validity (Tables 6–7). It also reports testing a third adversarial iteration without notable reward improvement (Section 4.5). These extend v2's retained validity/clipping ablations and two-iteration analysis with evidence about reward balance and continued training.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Dataset-averaged results and training curves retain the same uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1, v2 Table 3/v3 Table 8 and Figures 4–5 contain revised results. Figure 4 changes UTRL-4B/GPT-4.1 fidelity from 0.741/0.732 to 0.794/0.800, reversing their ranking. v3 adds results for the new benchmark, models, controls and ablations, while removing Figure 7's code-score results. Revised training budgets prevent interpreting all numerical changes as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and reward expressions in Section 3 and the PPO/GRPO objectives in Appendix A.1 are unchanged. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central claims: adversarial UTRL learns unit-test generation without ground-truth test labels, surpasses SFT and strong LLM baselines, and supports code-generator training. The added experiments do not redefine the headline contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations connecting reasoning-SFT's weak best-of-N results to less discriminative synthetic labels and interpreting the weight sweep as balancing validity and discrimination. It qualifies continued iterative improvement through the third-iteration plateau and conjectures that larger models could sustain progress. Appendix A.6's existing limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The v3 abstract adds a stated project page for code and materials beyond v2's future-release promise. Appendix A.3 newly specifies instruction-finetuned bases and UTRL-dagger's 100-step, single-iteration setup, alongside revised training schedules. Existing prompts, execution checks and optimizer hyperparameters are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantial adversarial-learning and self-play context covering GANs, symmetric/asymmetric self-play, AZR, SPIN, Sol-Ver and STP. This broadens the framework's research positioning beyond v2's unit-test-generation and RL discussion. LiveCodeBench is also newly cited, while the technical distinctions from CURE remain.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized rewrites in Sections 4.3–4.5, adds a related-work paragraph, organizes Appendix A.2 into numbered subsections and renames A.3. Conference headers and acknowledgements are added. The main narrative order, method exposition, conclusion and limitations are largely preserved.

P2.justification: v3 introduces Tables 3–7, expands Table 1 and redesigns Figure 7 from separate code-score/accuracy panels into one pass@1 plot with four training methods. Existing figures and tables are rearranged: v2 Table 3 becomes v3 Table 8, and Figures 9–11 are retained rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: Compared with v2, v3 strengthens validation through an independent benchmark, another model family, additional training controls and reward-balance experiments, while adding code-access information. The net gain is limited by reporting inconsistencies: Section 4.3 retains fidelity values 0.604/0.741 although Figure 5 now shows 0.648/0.794, and Table 6 incorrectly identifies lambda = 0 as omitting the validity reward. These issues reduce clarity and confidence in parts of the expanded evidence.
